(CNS) -- "Europe will miss an opportunity if it does not use the potential for mutually advantageous economic cooperation with China," former UNESCO Director-General Irina Bokova told China News Service's W.E. Talk when discussing China-EU relations.
Bokova, a recipient of the Lifetime Honorary Award at the second Orchid Awards, recently returned to China. She spoke about China-EU economic, trade and technological cooperation, ways to deepen understanding across cultures, and memories of her first visit to Shenzhen some 15 years ago.
She also expressed hope that the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting, to be held in Shenzhen later this month, would "serve as a bridge" to help ease mistrust and find solutions to pressing problems.
Asked about China-EU economic and trade frictions, Bokova said that amid geopolitical shifts, China's rise was not always understood in a non-confrontational way. Competition among countries would always exist, she noted, and the key was how to manage it.
"The most important thing, in my mind, is not to transform this into a confrontation."
She identified several areas for closer China-EU cooperation: joint scientific projects, exploring mutual transfers of technology, and technological innovation.
"China has a lot to offer Europe," she said. In her view, China's vast market and emerging technologies could also benefit Europe.
Bokova emphasized the need for closer cooperation amid major geopolitical shifts.
"China and Europe should aspire to become partners and not deepen the divisions that these geopolitical shifts are bringing to the world," she said.
She noted some positive signs in the relationship, while acknowledging that competition made further cooperation difficult. Negotiations would not always be easy, she said, but both sides should seek partnership, work through their differences, and avoid further divisions.
In October, the second meeting of the China-EU Trade and Investment Consultations and the 17th EU-China Joint Steering Committee Meeting on Science and Technology Cooperation were held in succession, covering trade and economic frictions, scientific and technological innovation, and cooperation mechanisms.
"We communicate with each other almost every single minute, but it doesn't mean that we have become more tolerant or more knowledgeable," Bokova said. More frequent communication, she noted, did not necessarily lead to greater mutual understanding.
"Communication does not automatically bring the results that we want."
She stressed the importance of education for cultural competence. Exchanges among museums, joint research by historians and scientists, exchanges of university students and professors, and visits to cultural sites in different countries could all help deepen understanding.
Bokova voiced strong support for China's visa-free policy for visitors from many European countries. She also mentioned China's initiatives to encourage visits by young people from abroad, support joint scientific projects, and attract international talent.
Involved with many universities herself, she said she had seen how important such exchanges were. People at different levels of society also needed to get to know one another to overcome possible prejudices and mistrust.
"It is not just governments that have to play a role," she said.
On China's international communication efforts, Bokova acknowledged renewed efforts in recent years while noting that they had not always achieved the desired results.
"Presenting Chinese culture and China's success to the world is a challenge, but it is a huge opportunity," she said.
She recalled visiting Chinese exhibitions marking the 60th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and France, noting the considerable impact they had made.
"I think that people have to come and see with their own eyes," she stressed.
By visiting China themselves, foreign visitors could see the country's development firsthand and gain a deeper understanding of Chinese traditions. Personal experience, in her view, could help people form their own understanding of China rather than rely solely on what some media present.
On her first visit to Shenzhen about 15 years ago, a bustling public reading space left a lasting impression on Bokova. People sat reading on the floor and in adjoining areas, while other spaces were set aside for children. She said she still had photographs from that visit.
"Shenzhen is a green city. Shenzhen is a learning city," she said.
In her view, the city's development since China's reform and opening-up has brought together universities, technology, culture and finance, reflecting an emphasis on learning, science and technology, and inclusive development.
The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen on Nov. 18 and 19.
Bokova noted that the Asia-Pacific region was growing economically, with many countries embracing technological development. The United States and Russia were also important players in the region. Amid complex regional challenges, countries needed more opportunities for dialogue and cooperation.
She said the world faced multiple challenges, with progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals falling short, alongside climate change and geopolitical shifts. Against this backdrop, she emphasized China's role as an important supporter of the United Nations and multilateralism.
"There is definitely a need for more dialogue," Bokova said.
"I hope that this meeting here will serve as a bridge," she added, expressing hope that the APEC meeting in Shenzhen could help ease mistrust and find solutions to pressing problems.
"I think that today, the attention of many people around the world is very much focused on Shenzhen," Bokova said.
Irina Bokova is former Director-General of the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and Senior Advisor to the Board of Directors of the Europe-Asia Center.
She served as UNESCO Director-General from 2009 to 2017. During her tenure, she helped facilitate the inclusion of 11 Chinese cities in the UNESCO Creative Cities Network and nine major Chinese cultural heritage sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List. She also played a key role in establishing the UNESCO Prize for Girls' and Women's Education in cooperation with China.
In 2016, Bokova was named to Forbes' list of the World's 100 Most Powerful Women. In 2020, she was elected an International Honorary Member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2025, she received the Lifetime Honorary Award at the second Orchid Awards and the 2025 Chinese Government Friendship Award.

articles.fullText:
People paddleboard as a container ship is seen in the distance in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, November 14, 2026. 
Iran on Sunday rejected demands by Gulf states that it pay compensation for damage attributed to its attacks in the region. Meanwhile, Bahrain said its air defense systems had intercepted several Iranian drones, while Tehran claimed to have targeted a US radar installation in the kingdom, amid continued tensions over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said regional countries that had "actively participated in the military aggression" against Iran and allowed their territories to be used by the United States and Israel could not demand reparations.
Speaking at a weekly press conference, Baghaei said Iran was instead seeking compensation for losses and damage it said had been inflicted on the country, adding that Tehran had documented the relevant cases. He maintained that Iran's retaliatory actions were "purely defensive in nature" and targeted only US military bases and assets used to launch attacks against Iran.
The remarks followed a call by Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi for Iran to provide full compensation for damage, losses and injuries resulting from its attacks on Gulf states. Addressing the UN Security Council on Friday, Albudaiwi said GCC countries had faced more than 7,000 Iranian missiles and drones since February 28, targeting airports, ports, energy facilities, water desalination plants and civilian infrastructure. He held Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences.
Meanwhile, Bahrain's Defense Force said on Sunday that its air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed several Iranian drones before they reached their targets. The announcement came after the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said its aerospace force had targeted a US air defense radar installation at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain with six drones. The claimed strike had not been independently confirmed, with no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities.
Bahrain's Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks as violations of the kingdom's sovereignty and international law, saying it reserved the right to self-defense. Separately, the IRGC Navy said two oil tankers had exploded after striking naval mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz through what it called an unauthorized route.
On the diplomatic front, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported, citing Baghaei, that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi would travel to Muscat on Tuesday for talks with his Omani counterpart.
Earlier this month, Araghchi described Qatari-mediated indirect talks between Tehran and Washington as "very intense," although they ended without significant progress toward an agreement. He said the future of diplomatic efforts depended on the US's "political rationality" and warned that any renewed military action against Iran would be met with a heavy response.
The disruption to shipping through the strait has also raised concerns over global food security. Jorge Moreira da Silva, executive director of the UN Office for Project Services (UNOPS), said on Saturday that Iran and the United States should immediately allow fertilizer shipments to pass through the waterway to ease pressure on vulnerable countries.
Before the conflict, about one-third of the world's fertilizers were transported through the Strait of Hormuz, while fertilizer prices have risen by around 30% since the blockades began, he said. Calling for at least five fertilizer vessels to be allowed through the strait each day, da Silva warned that continued disruption could leave 45 million people facing severe and acute food insecurity and push another 30 million into poverty if planting seasons are missed. He added that the UN had a system ready to get fertilizer shipments moving within seven to ten days.

The Antalya Leaders' Summit of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) opened on Wednesday, with a focus on turning climate commitments into concrete action.
Opening the high-level meeting, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged international cooperation on shared challenges. "We do not need countries to agree on everything, but we do need them to cooperate on the things no country can solve alone," he said.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres delivers a speech during the Leaders' Summit of the COP31 in Antalya, Turkiye, November 11, 2026. 
Guterres noted that global emissions reached a record high in 2025 and that the past four years were the hottest in history. Pointing out that fossil fuels must be phased out, he stated that major oil companies should contribute to recovery efforts through taxes on their windfall profits.
Highlighting the transition in the energy sector, Guterres added that solar power alone met nearly three quarters of the growth in global electricity demand last year, proving that clean energy has become the cheapest source of new electricity across most of the world.
This year's summit aims to bridge the gap between ambition and delivery by focusing on implementation, finance delivery and climate resilience.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stressed that prioritizing the needs of Pacific Island nations was a key responsibility. He called for climate finance to become more accessible, predictable, and responsive to actual needs.
"Developed nations, which have historically consumed the global carbon budget, must assume greater responsibility in both emission reductions and financing," Erdogan said.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese emphasized that international cooperation is unlocking clean energy investments and accelerating climate finance, while stressing that "no one must be left behind" in the transition.
Pointing to progress since the Paris Agreement, with projected warming dropping from 4 degrees Celsius to around 2.6 degrees, Albanese urged leaders to treat this decade as a critical window to keep the 1.5 degrees Celsius goal within reach and turn ambition into implementation.

A new international study has found that the global cryosphere is degrading at an accelerating pace, with some changes potentially irreversible, posing long-term risks to Earth's ecosystems and human societies.
The cryosphere, which includes glaciers, ice sheets, permafrost, sea ice and snow cover, holds about 70% of the Earth's freshwater resources, but is rapidly shrinking. Its degradation has already affected water security, ecosystems and infrastructure worldwide.
Researchers from Stockholm University in Sweden, Tsinghua University in China, the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany and other institutions and international organizations published the study on the journal Science on Friday.
Using the planetary boundaries framework, the researchers systematically assessed the role of the cryosphere in maintaining the stability of the Earth system. They defined its safe operating space based on the Holocene, which began about 11,700 years ago and was characterized by relatively stable climate and environmental conditions.
The study found that the global cryosphere has exceeded its safe operating space and is degrading at an accelerating pace, with some changes potentially irreversible. Some key indicators have already deviated from the relatively stable conditions of the Holocene, while further deviations in other indicators are becoming increasingly difficult to avoid.
The reinforcing interactions between cryosphere degradation and global warming could further accelerate the trend, exposing human societies and ecosystems to long-term risks.
Researchers warned that the cryosphere's transgression of its safe operating space means the frozen environmental foundations that have supported human civilization for thousands of years are under threat.
The study identified human-induced climate change as the main driver of cryosphere degradation, while black carbon emissions, industrial activities and infrastructure expansion further intensify degradation in some regions.
Researchers called on countries to adopt more ambitious emission reduction targets and reduce human disturbances in cryosphere-sensitive areas.
